new_statements.quote: The resulting array is not unlike those of other Baja langusges. Despite the stress mark on the language's name, there is no other record suggesting that stress in Pericú was on the final syllable of a phonological word, but the possibility of this is likely. new_statements.rule_in_words: The only analyst to address the question says outright that there is no record of Pericú stress: the dozen surviving words (1632 Carbonel/Ortega list, Parra 1683, one Jesuit item) carry no accent marks. His guess that stress fell on the last syllable of the phonological word rests only on the acute accent in the Spanish-recorded name 'Pericú' and on areal analogy with Cochimí, Robinia and Monqui (final/last-syllable stress), and he brackets it as '[perhaps final]'. This is a documented absence of evidence with a hedged final-stress conjecture, not a description of a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('no other record', 'possibility... is likely', '[perhaps final]').
new_statements.domain_note: 'Phonological word' in Shaul's Baja framework (for Cochimí it can span a close-knit phrase). Based entirely on 17th-18th-century written wordlist material; no speakers since the 18th century, no texts, no marked accents.
new_statements.identity_note: Pericú proper (peri1250), the language of the Cape region south of the Tropic (Cabo San Lucas-San José del Cabo-Santiago) and of the Gulf islands (Isleños of Cerralvo, Espíritu Santo, San José; Massey 1949). The surviving words come from Espíritu Santo islanders (Carbonel de Valenzuela/Ortega 1632, Parra 1683) plus one Jesuit item ('miñicari'); Shaul 2020 analyses exactly this corpus (León-Portilla 1976). Neighbouring Cape languages Huchití/Uchití and Cora (Huchití-speaking per Massey) and Monqui are separate varieties without glottocodes and are not involved. No dialect issue beyond the island/mainland split, on which no linguistic difference is recorded.

sources.note: Ch. 8 re-analyses the dozen words assembled by León-Portilla 1976 (aynu, boxo, eni, ipiri, ipiri-ka, itawriwi, kadwaño, miñikari, nakwi, unoa, uri, utere, waxoro), gives vowels /i e u o a/ and a consonant array, and then says (p. 38, PDF 46): 'Despite the stress mark on the language's name, there is no other record suggesting that stress in Pericú was on the final syllable of a phonological word, but the possibility of this is likely.' The areal table on p. 50 (PDF 58) gives Pericú stress as '[perhaps final]' (brackets = inferred), and p. 4 counts 'main stress placement' among the areal trait…

sources.note: The web page (read in full) lists 11 Pericú toponyms with sources (Aiñiní, Anicá, Añuití, Caduaño, Calluco, Cunimniici, Eguí, Marinó, Purum, Yeneca, Yenecamú) and nothing on stress; Google Books snippets of the 1997 chapter (id 1ruEAAAAIAAJ, pp. 79-80 Pericú territory list) show the same toponym list and discussion of Cora-Pericú boundaries, no phonology.

sources.citation: Massey, William C. 1949. Tribes and Languages of Baja California. Southwestern Journal of Anthropology 5(3): 272-307. Pericú entry pp. 279-283.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnohistorical: Pericú a language 'distinct from all others on the peninsula' (Taraval, Barco), territory, three rancheria names (Anica, Yeneca, Puurum), place names Caduaño 'arroyo verde' and Calluco, 'Guaxoro' = friend (p. 283); Porter Casanate's 1649 vocabulary 'is not extant'. No remark on pronunciation or accent.

sources.citation: Clavigero, Francesco Saverio. 1789. Storia della California. Venezia: Modesto Fenzo. Lib. I, section on the nations and languages.
sources.note: Nothing: 'La lingua Pericù è oggimai estinta, e que' pochi, che vi restano di quella sventurata Nazione, parlano lo Spagnuolo'; Pericú located from Cabo San Lucas to 24° and the islands; no Pericú data. Buschmann 1859 (bub_gb_R99EAAAAcAAJ), Pimentel 1874 ('La lengua pericú ya no existe') and Baegert 1772/1865/1952 (guai1237 folder) were also grepped: Pericú only as an ethnonym/language name, no data.
